question: Six hours after delivery, a 3050-g (6-lb 12-oz) male newborn is noted to have feeding intolerance and several episodes of bilious vomiting. He was born at term to a healthy 35-year-old woman following a normal vaginal delivery. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, but the patient's mother had missed several of her prenatal checkups. The patient's older brother underwent surgery for pyloric stenosis as an infant. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows epicanthus, upward slanting of the eyelids, low-set ears, and a single transverse palmar crease. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the left mid to lower sternal border. Abdominal examination shows a distended upper abdomen and a concave-shaped lower abdomen. There is no organomegaly. An x-ray of the abdomen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Feeding intolerance and bilious vomiting" -> "Possible gastrointestinal obstruction" -> "Consider congenital anomaly" -> 70% CHAIN: "Epicanthus, upward slanting of the eyelids, low-set ears, single transverse palmar crease" -> "Suspicion of genetic syndrome" -> "Increased risk for congenital anomalies" -> 80% CHAIN: "Grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur at left sternal border" -> "Possible cardiac anomaly" -> "Consider associated syndromes" -> 70% CHAIN: "Distended upper abdomen, concave-shaped lower abdomen" -> "Abdominal asymmetry" -> "Suggestive of gastrointestinal obstruction" -> 75% CHAIN: "Family history of pyloric stenosis in older brother" -> "Increased risk for pyloric stenosis" -> "Consider pyloric stenosis as a differential diagnosis" -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the newborn with feeding intolerance, bilious vomiting, physical findings suggestive of a genetic syndrome, and a family history of pyloric stenosis in the older brother is Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (opd). The presence of a distended upper abdomen and concave-shaped lower abdomen further supports this diagnosis.
analysis: The newborn presents with feeding intolerance, bilious vomiting, physical features suggestive of a genetic syndrome, and a family history of pyloric stenosis in the older brother. The combination of symptoms and findings, including a distended upper abdomen and concave-shaped lower abdomen, is highly indicative of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. This condition commonly presents in male infants around 3-6 weeks of age with non-bilious projectile vomiting. The presence of a holosystolic murmur is likely an incidental finding. Other options like duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung's disease, necrotizing enterocolitis, and meconium ileus are less likely based on the clinical presentation and family history.
